title: Eighteen years addicted
summary: He did not know he could get dependent; it interfered with his creativity for eighteen years.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: That was the beginning of it then. I got back into New York and I was so naive, I had no idea that you could get physically dependent on it, that you could get sick, that you could get strung out; I had no idea of those things. I thought it was a thing you tried, like sucking a lollipop. You eat it and that's it.
There wasn't discussion of this on the band?
No. I hadn't heard it. Maybe I'd hear talk about somebody being sick, but I thought they were referring to somebody having a cold.

I got to like it and I became more and more involved with it and then I was doing it all the time, still not knowing that I really had to do it at that time, because if I didn't I would have really gotten into bad shape, if I had let any time go by.
How did you pay for it? Was it expensive, where did you buy it?
I had money to begin with, I always managed to earn some money.
Was it easy to buy?
Very easy; it was everywhere.
I really don't want to talk about this, Bill, because I don't think it did anything but interfere with my creativity for eighteen years, until I got out of it.
Is there anything specially musical about dope?
No.
Postmen, in those days didn't get involved with dope.
Who?
Postment, or trolley operators, at least it wasn't a vocational thing, or air mail pilots. Musicians seem to have a special relationship with dope; why would that be?

I don't know, Bill, I think it's part of the life; the hours that you work, the type of people that exist in that world, part of the tension, the pressure of the world requires some kind of outside help. I think people are strong and people are weak; the weak ones reach out for help, the strong ones learn or the smart ones learn to make it on their own, come what may and if it hurts, you're supposed to let it hurt; that's part of it. You don't hide from pain. That particular way brought a new pain all the time.
At some point you broke loose from that.
It took a long time, and it took--like I said, it lasted eighteen

years; it was eighteen years of being addicted and trying to become unaddicted. I got that way, couldn't stand it and broke myself of it, which was a tortuous process, got out of it and got immediately right back in. Boom, boom, boom. Eighteen years.
It's really strange that I managed to get some work done during that time.
The work you did during that time was, in many ways, the best you've ever done.
Right.
